name: Furazabol

lead: Furazabol is an oral anabolic-androgenic steroid marketed in Japan since 1969, structurally nearly identical to stanozolol with a furazan ring in place of its pyrazole ring. Bodybuilders discuss it for lean mass and strength.

It is a 17α-alkylated DHT derivative acting on the androgen receptor, reported to have a relatively high anabolic-to-androgenic ratio. Rat studies reported effects on blood fibrinolysis, and it has been described as lipid-lowering, though author William Llewellyn regards that as a myth. Sources are mostly doping-control and animal studies; in North America it became known through the Dubin Inquiry into Ben Johnson's 1988 case.

paras: It was used orally as a medicine in Japan. Physique use is based on discussion rather than documented routines.
As a 17α-alkylated steroid it may carry a risk of liver toxicity. It is Schedule III in the United States and Schedule IV in Canada, and anabolic steroids are prohibited in sport.

angle.text: Furazabol is discussed for lean mass and strength: as an oral stanozolol-like steroid it activates androgen receptors and is reported to have a high anabolic-to-androgenic ratio. Sources are mostly doping and animal studies, with no modern human trials.

lead: Furazabol is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid that has been marketed in Japan since 1969. It is a 17α-alkylated derivative of dihydrotestosterone and is structurally close to stanozolol, differing in having a furazan ring where stanozolol has a pyrazole ring. [1]

Wikipedia reports a relatively high anabolic-to-androgenic ratio and describes antihyperlipidemic properties, which the author William Llewellyn regards as a myth. [1] Published sources on furazabol are largely animal pharmacology and analytical studies for doping control rather than human efficacy trials. [2][3]
In North America furazabol became known through the Dubin Inquiry into the 1988 Olympic doping case of sprinter Ben Johnson. [1]

paras: Early Japanese work described the metabolites of furazabol in rats and some non-hormonal properties of the compound. [4][5] A 1976 rat study reported that treatment enhanced fibrinolytic and thrombolytic potential. [6] A 1980 rat study found that furazabol, among other anabolic steroids, altered the level of cytosolic androgen receptor in the prostate of castrated animals. [7]
Wikipedia lists a half-life of about four hours, noting the figure lacks a citation. [1] Human urine excretion studies were later published for doping control. [8][9]
Like other 17α-alkylated anabolic steroids, furazabol may carry a risk of hepatotoxicity. [1]

Furazabol was little known among North American athletes until the Dubin Inquiry. After winning the 100 m at the 1988 Seoul Olympics, Ben Johnson tested positive for stanozolol and was stripped of his medal. He later claimed to have been taking furazabol, which he said could not be detected. His physician testified that he supplied furazabol, but a vial that sprinter Angella Issajenko believed held furazabol proved to contain stanozolol. The Commission concluded that stanozolol had been supplied and that furazabol was either imagined or a fabrication. [1]
Analytical chemistry papers have described detection of furazabol in human urine and in racehorse doping tests. [3][8][9]
Furazabol has the formula C20H30N2O2. Its metabolism includes 17-epimerization like other 17α-methyl anabolic steroids. [1][10]
No studies found of furazabol for muscle or appearance outcomes. Available research consists of rat pharmacology and doping-detection studies in humans and horses. [3][6][8]

timeline.event: Ben Johnson claims furazabol use after his stanozolol positive at the Seoul Olympics; the Dubin Inquiry later concluded stanozolol had been supplied. [1]
